sections.category: Thinking Machines releases Inkling, a 975B open-weights multimodal MoE built to be fine-tuned rather than rented, with a 276B Inkling-Small preview alongside

bullets.body: Mira Murati's Thinking Machines Lab on July 15 released Inkling, its first from-scratch model, as open weights. The architecture is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 975B total parameters and 41B active per token, pretrained on 45 trillion tokens spanning text, images, audio, and video, with a context window up to 1M tokens; a 276B-total / 12B-active Inkling-Small preview ships with the same recipe for latency-sensitive work. The lab is explicit that Inkling is not the strongest model available, open or closed — the bet is that enterprises want a customizable base rather than a rented frontier endpoint, and the release routes directly into Tinker, the company's fine-tuning platform, where Inkling is available at 64K and 256K context options. Distribution was coordinated: Together AI served Inkling on day 0 behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint handling text, image, and audio input with per-request reasoning-effort control. For the local-LLM ecosystem the significance is a second US neolab (after the summer's Chinese MoE wave) putting a frontier-scale trained-from-scratch model under open weights with fine-tuning as the explicit business model rather than an afterthought.

sections.category: Unsloth ships v0.1.49-beta with same-day Inkling support, a four-level tool-call permission system, and Vulkan-backed Intel GPU inference

bullets.body: Unsloth's v0.1.49-beta release, published July 15, lands Inkling — the new 975B-total / 41B-active open model with up to a 1M context window — in the same news cycle as the model itself, continuing the project's pattern of same-day support for major open-weight drops. The security-relevant change is a four-level tool-call permission selector (Ask, Approve for me, Off, Full access) with workspace isolation, replacing the previous binary toggle — a notable convergence of fine-tuning tooling toward the permission-gating vocabulary that coding agents adopted after this year's agent-exfiltration incidents. Hardware reach also widens: Intel GPUs get GPU-accelerated inference through new Vulkan llama.cpp support where they were previously CPU-bound, and the NVFP4 model collection grows with dynamic NVFP4 support, extending the post-training NVFP4/FP8/imatrix-GGUF export path that shipped in v0.1.48 on July 7.

sections.category: Microsoft's record 570-CVE Patch Tuesday carries a critical Copilot remote-code-execution flaw and a GitHub Copilot / VS Code cluster, with AI-assisted discovery cited as the volume driver

bullets.body: Microsoft's July 14 Patch Tuesday fixed a record 570 vulnerabilities, including three zero-days of which two were exploited in the wild. The AI-surface cluster is the part worth reading closely: CVE-2026-48561 is a critical remote-code-execution flaw in Microsoft Copilot itself, joined by a GitHub Copilot RCE (CVE-2026-50510), a Copilot / VS Code security-feature bypass (CVE-2026-41109), and a Copilot / VS Code token-disclosure flaw (CVE-2026-47282) — the assistant and the editor it lives in are now a recurring Patch Tuesday category rather than an exotic one-off. Fifty-nine of the 570 are rated critical, 48 of those RCEs, with multiple entries above CVSS 8.0 across Windows Media Foundation, DirectX, and DHCP. The stated reason for the volume is itself an AI story: Microsoft attributes the surge to its AI-powered internal vulnerability-discovery system, and Adobe moved to twice-monthly bulletins effective the same day, citing AI-accelerated discovery compressing the disclosure-to-exploitation window.

citations.label: BleepingComputer - Microsoft July 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes massive 570 flaws, 3 zero-days

sections.category: xAI open-sources the entire Grok Build coding agent under Apache 2.0 after the wire-level upload teardown, disabling the Google Cloud directory-upload path outright

bullets.body: xAI answered this week's wire-level teardown of its Grok build CLI — which showed repositories, git history, and unredacted .env secrets flowing to a Google Cloud bucket — by open-sourcing the whole agent as xai-org/grok-build under Apache 2.0 on July 15: 844,530 lines of Rust, roughly 97% original code, published as a periodically-synced export of the internal monorepo. The upload feature that triggered the backlash is disabled, with the remnant Google Cloud code now returning hardcoded unavailability errors, and the release pitches local-first operation with data retention off. Simon Willison's read-through of the codebase surfaces the details vendors usually keep private: the full agent and subagent system prompts (the subagent is instructed to conceal its own prompt from users), tool implementations ported from competing agents including Codex and Claude Code, and a codebase materially larger than the terminal-agent norm. As a disclosure-driven outcome it is the strongest of the year's agent-trust incidents so far — full source publication, not a changelog apology — and it hands security researchers a rare complete reference for how a shipping agent actually wires uploads, tool calls, and permissions.

citations.label: Simon Willison - xAI open-sources Grok Build

sections.category: TSMC posts a record quarter on AI demand — revenue up 36% and net income up 77% year-over-year — as 2nm reaches 3% of wafer revenue in its first reported quarter

bullets.body: TSMC's second-quarter results, published July 16, quantify how far AI accelerator demand is pulling the foundry: revenue of NT$1,270.38 billion (US$40.20 billion, up 36.0% year-over-year in NT terms and 12.0% sequentially), net income of NT$706.56 billion up 77.4%, and margins that would have been implausible for a foundry two years ago — 67.7% gross, 60.3% operating, 55.6% net. The node mix is the forward-looking signal: 2-nanometer contributed 3% of wafer revenue in its first meaningful quarter, 3nm held 30%, and advanced nodes (7nm and below) took 77% of the total. CFO Wendell Huang guided Q3 to US$44.6-45.8 billion on "the steep ramp-up of our 2-nanometer technology," and the company raised its 2026 capital-spending plan to the US$60-64 billion range. For everyone downstream — NVIDIA and AMD accelerator allocations, hyperscaler build schedules, and the on-device NPU roadmaps that ride the same leading-edge capacity — the constraint picture stays the same: demand is being rationed by wafer supply, and TSMC is spending accordingly.

sections.category: AI events to plan around now: the AGI Summit opens in San Francisco this weekend, AMD Advancing AI follows July 22-23, and OpenAI DevDay lands September 29 at Fort Mason on an already-crowded late-September calendar

bullets.body: The nearest decision is unchanged and now urgent: the AGI Summit runs July 18-19 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco, this coming weekend, with AMD Advancing AI 2026 at Moscone West on July 22-23 right behind it, where Lisa Su and partners are expected to detail the Instinct MI450 accelerator and Zen 6 EPYC "Venice" CPUs. The AI-chip and infrastructure track then runs Hot Chips at Stanford on August 23-25 — early registration closes July 31 — and the AI Infra Summit at the Santa Clara Convention Center on September 15-17. The AI-security block clusters from early August: Black Hat USA and DEF CON 34's AI Village in Las Vegas August 1-6, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit in Half Moon Bay August 11-12, OWASP Global AppSec USA in San Francisco November 5-6, and Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series for agent-hijack and MCP-layer defense teams. On the developer and data track: Ai4 2026 at The Venetian in Las Vegas August 4-6, Anyscale's Ray Summit August 24-26 at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis, the AI Tinkerers San Francisco meetup in August, the ACM AI Leadership Summit in Atlanta August 30-September 2, The AI Conference at Pier 48 September 29-October 1, the Runway AI Summit at The Masonic September 30, World Summit AI in Amsterdam October 7-8, GitHub Universe October 28-29, AWS re:Invent November 30-December 4, NeurIPS in December, IEEE-RAS Humanoids at the Santa Clara Convention Center December 7-9, and The AI Summit New York December 9-10 closing the year. Two additions this week: OpenAI DevDay 2026 is set for Tuesday, September 29 at Fort Mason in San Francisco — in-person applications are already closed ($650 for those selected), the keynote streams free with sign-up, and DevDay Exchanges follow in eight cities including Tokyo, Berlin, and London later in the year — which stacks the same September 29 date as The AI Conference's Day Zero and the eve of the Runway AI Summit into one San Francisco super-week; and PyTorch Conference North America 2026 runs October 20-21 in San Jose, covering PyTorch, vLLM, DeepSpeed, and Ray with security and full-stack tracks, with discounted early registration open now. Near-term actions: decide on the AGI Summit before Saturday, register for AMD Advancing AI ahead of July 22, lock the July 31 Hot Chips early rate, book the early-August Las Vegas security block, and pick a lane for the September 29 collision — DevDay keynote sign-up costs nothing even if you attend Pier 48 instead.
